title: Accuracy is not enough
objectives: Use precision, recall and the ROC curve on unbalanced classes
Read AUC as a ranking probability
Compare classifiers across thresholds, not at one each

screens.prose: A lender looks back at 1,000 recent firms: 50 defaulted within a year and 950 repaid. The laziest model needs no data at all: it says “no default” for every firm.
screens.question: What share of firms does “always no” classify correctly?

widget.label: Share correct
widget.accept: 95%: it is right on the 950 firms that repaid.

hints.text: Which firms does “no default” get right?
It is right on every firm that repaid.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the firms for which “no default” is the truth.

byKey.five: 5% is the share that defaulted, and “always no” gets every one of those wrong.
byKey.half: Two answers does not mean half right. 950 firms really did repay.

explain.text: “Always no” scores 95% **accuracy** and catches no default at all. Our logistic regression, cut at 0.5, scores 94.9%: worse than doing nothing. When one class is rare, accuracy mostly measures the base rate.

screens.prose: Our logistic regression scores each of the 1,000 firms; the scores came from fitting on 1,000 earlier firms. Cut at a threshold of 0.1, it flags 150 firms, and 29 of those defaulted. Remember 50 firms defaulted in all.
screens.question: Fill in the rest of the table.

The flagged row adds to 150; the defaulted column adds to 50.
Flagged and repaid: $150 - 29 = 121$. Not flagged and defaulted: $50 - 29 = 21$. The rest: $1{,}000 - 29 - 121 - 21 = 829$.

feedback.correct: 121, 21 and 829: the four cells add to 1,000.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the totals: 150 flagged, 50 defaulted, 1,000 firms.

byKey.r0c2: Of 150 flagged firms 29 defaulted, so $150 - 29 = 121$ repaid.

explain.text: This table is the **confusion matrix**: rows are what the model said, columns what happened. Its accuracy is $(29 + 829)/1{,}000 = 85.8\%$, below “always no”. Yet it catches 29 of the 50 defaults.

screens.prose: Two questions matter more than accuracy here. Of the firms we flagged, what share defaulted? Of the firms that defaulted, what share did we flag? The table is the one you just filled.
screens.question: Fill in the three numbers, to 3 decimal places.

rows: share of flagged firms that defaulted
share of defaults that were flagged

hints.text: Each share has 29 on top.
Flagged firms: 150. Defaults: 50.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 29 by the flagged total, then by the default total.

explain.text: The first is **precision**, $\text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FP})$; the second is **recall**, $\text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FN})$; the third is **F1**. “Always no” has recall 0, which accuracy hid. scikit-learn has `precision_score`, `recall_score` and `f1_score`.

screens.prose: Each threshold gives one point: the share of survivors wrongly flagged across, the share of defaults caught up. Sweep the threshold and the point traces the **ROC curve**. The slider moves the threshold from 0 (step 0) up to 0.8.

screens.question: Slide the threshold all the way down to 0. Where does the point end up, and what is the precision there?

options.text: At (1, 1): every firm flagged, recall 1 and precision 0.05, the base rate

options.why: That is the top threshold. At 0 every score is at least the threshold, so every firm is flagged.
Recall is 1 because every default is flagged, but so is every survivor. Precision is $50/1{,}000 = 0.05$.
(0, 1) would catch every default with no false alarms. No threshold of ours gets there.

hints.text: At $t = 0$, which firms are flagged?
Every firm is flagged, defaulters and survivors alike.
Recall $= 50/50 = 1$, false positive rate $= 950/950 = 1$, precision $= 50/1{,}000 = 0.05$.

feedback.correct: At $t = 0$ recall is 1 and precision falls to the base rate, 0.05.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the slider to step 0 and read the caption.

explain.text: A threshold of 0 flags everyone: recall 1, false positive rate 1, precision 0.05. Recall alone is easy to max out. The curve shows what each extra default costs in false alarms.

screens.prose: Pick one firm that defaulted and one that repaid. How often does the model score the defaulter higher? Here are 4 defaulters and 5 survivors from the test set with their scores.
screens.question: Of the 20 defaulter–survivor pairs, in what fraction is the defaulter scored higher?

0.357, 0.126 and 0.085 are above all five survivors.

screens.prose: Two teams report on the same 1,000 firms. Team A: recall 0.16, precision 0.38. Team B: recall 0.78, precision 0.12. Team B says its model is better because it catches 39 of 50 defaults, not 8.
screens.question: What can you conclude from these two reports?

options.text: B's model is better: it catches far more defaults
options.why: You compared recall at two different thresholds. Any model catches more defaults when its threshold is lower.

options.text: A's model is better: its precision is three times higher
options.why: A higher threshold always raises precision. You compared two settings, not two models.

options.text: Nothing yet: compare the two ranking curves, or each model's recall at the same false positive rate
A's model is better: its F1 is 0.23 against 0.21
options.why: F1 depends on the threshold too. Both teams picked their own.

hints.text: Where would each report sit on an ROC chart?
A lower threshold moves a model's point up and to the right along its own curve.
Both points lie on our model's ROC curve: A is $t = 0.3$ and B is $t = 0.05$. The same model, two thresholds.

feedback.correct: A threshold is a setting; compare models across all thresholds, or at one false positive rate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the two reports used the same threshold.

byKey.b: You compared recall at two different thresholds. Any model catches more defaults when its threshold is lower.

explain.text: Both reports are our own model: A is $t = 0.3$ and B is $t = 0.05$, two points on one ROC curve. Comparing models needs the whole curve (AUC) or one fixed operating point. AUC is not accuracy: 0.828 means a ranking, not 82.8% of firms right.

screens.question: A model that ranks firms at random flags defaulters in proportion. What precision does it have, at any recall?

hints.text: A random ranking flags defaulters and survivors in the proportions they occur.
Among all firms, 50 of 1,000 defaulted.
Any random sample of firms is 5% defaulters: precision 0.05.

feedback.correct: A random ranking's precision is the base rate, 0.05.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What share of a random sample of firms defaulted?

byKey.half: 0.5 is a coin's AUC. A coin's precision is the share of positives, here 0.05.
byKey.one: Precision 1 means every flagged firm defaulted. A random ranking flags mostly survivors.

explain.text: On the ROC chart a coin sits at AUC 0.5 whatever the base rate. On the precision-recall chart its line sits at the base rate, so rare positives look as hard as they are. Our model's precision at recall 0.58 is 0.19: about 4 times the base rate.

screens.prose: Now in code. If nothing is flagged, return 0.0 for precision, as `precision_score` does with `zero_division=0`. `y_test` and `p_test` hold the 1,000 firms' outcomes and scores.
screens.question: Complete `precision_recall(y, yhat)`.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 2000
lev = np.round(rng.normal(0, 1, n), 3)
cover = np.round(rng.normal(0, 1, n), 3)
z = -4.4 + 1.5 * lev - 1.0 * cover
default = (rng.uniform(0, 1, n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
score = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(-3.703 + 1.210 * lev[1000:] - 0.765 * cover[1000:])))
y_test = [int(v) for v in default[1000:]]
p_test = [round(float(v), 4) for v in score]

tests.call: [round(v, 4) for v in precision_recall(y_test, [1 if v >= 0.1 else 0 for v in p_test])]

screens.prose: Write the points of the ROC curve. For each threshold, flag every score at or above it. FPR is false positives over all survivors; TPR is recall.
screens.question: Complete `roc_points(y, p, thresholds)`.

widget.solution:
def roc_points(y, p, thresholds):
    # for each t: flag p >= t; return [(fpr, tpr), ...] rounded to 4 places
    pos = sum(y)
    neg = len(y) - pos
    out = []
    for t in thresholds:
        tp = sum(1 for a, b in zip(y, p) if a == 1 and b >= t)
        fp = sum(1 for a, b in zip(y, p) if a == 0 and b >= t)
        out.append((round(fp / neg, 4), round(tp / pos, 4)))
    return out

screens.prose: A signal tries to flag “big up days”, returns above 2%, which are 4% of days. Over 1,000 days there were 40 big up days. The signal fired on 20 days and was right on 11: precision 0.55, almost 14 times the base rate.
screens.question: What is the signal's recall?

widget.label: Recall
widget.accept: 0.275: it caught 11 of the 40 big up days.

hints.text: Recall asks about the big up days, not about the firings.
There were 40 big up days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the hits by the number of big up days.

byKey.prec: 0.55 is precision, 11 of 20 firings. Recall divides by the 40 big up days.
byKey.fires: 0.02 is how often it fires, 20 of 1,000 days.

explain.text: The signal misses 29 of 40 big days and fires twice a month. Its precision rests on 20 firings, so its standard error is $\sqrt{0.55 \times 0.45/20} = 0.11$. Precision far above the base rate is promising; 20 trades are not yet proof.

ideas: With rare positives, accuracy mostly measures the base rate: “always no” scores 95% and catches nothing.
Precision divides the hits by what was flagged; recall divides them by what was positive. A threshold trades one for the other.
The ROC curve sweeps every threshold; AUC is the chance a random positive outranks a random negative, 0.5 for a coin.
summary.trap: Judging a rare-event model by accuracy, or comparing two models at different thresholds.

That would be precision. At $t = 0.1$ ours is 0.19.

quiz.prose: At a threshold of 0.05 our model flags 313 firms, 39 of which defaulted. 50 firms defaulted in all.
quiz.question: What are precision and recall?

options.why: You swapped them. Precision divides by the 313 flagged; recall by the 50 defaults.
39/1,000 divides by every firm. Precision divides by the firms flagged.
0.29 is the false positive rate, 274/950. Recall is 39/50.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Precision is 39 over the flagged; recall is 39 over the defaults.

explain.text: $39/313 = 0.125$ and $39/50 = 0.78$. A low threshold buys recall with precision.
